title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory, artifact‑backed outcomes: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We emphasize up front that two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation semantics and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—produced a ceiling effect that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for this run. We present the artifact‑backed execution and analysis, diagnose why the design produced a null outcome, and provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for hardening action‑aware benchmarks to expose generator×guard dynamics.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks that translate operator intent into device configurations and staged rollouts (canaries, progressive delivery, rollback). Prior prototypes and surveys report promise but also warn that operational safety requires end‑to‑end evaluation that includes generation, deterministic verification, staged rollout semantics, rollback, and provenance. Motivated by this evaluation gap, we preregistered and executed a paired experiment (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) to test whether adding a deterministic runtime validator to an LLM pipeline increases end‑to‑end safety (safe‑deploy rate) versus an LLM‑only pipeline.

Research question. Under a tightly controlled action‑aware staging benchmark, does a verifier‑augmented pipeline increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline). The N=400 paired design and analysis plan were frozen before execution.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented and LLM‑only pipeline on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1; (2) complete execution and analysis artifacts (execution/* and analysis/*) that reproduce the reported numbers; (3) a focused diagnosis explaining why two preregistered design choices produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run; (4) concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark hardening to reveal generator×guard interactions in future runs.
sections.related_work: Intent translation, LLM‑driven configuration synthesis, and verifier‑guided IaC workflows are active research areas. Recent work demonstrates LLMs can produce configuration‑style outputs in prototype and benchmark settings (intent→configuration studies and PreConfig/GraphSynth prototypes) while IaC systems show value from verifier‑guided feedback. Deterministic network verification and reachability tools can reliably detect configuration errors offline; these tools have been proposed as runtime guards. Agentic, tool‑augmented architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) are applied to AIOps and NetOps but introduce new failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployment patterns. Surveys emphasize a shortage of standardized, action‑aware benchmarks that include rollout, blocking, repair, rollback, and provenance; our study operationalizes a compact staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe verifier utility. The cited literature motivates our design choices (paired inference, staged semantics, verifier use) and underpins our recommendations for benchmark hardening.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with exactly N=400 deterministic tasks produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = permutation‑based paired test (two‑sided, α=0.05). The preregistration and analysis plan, including seeds and resampling counts, were frozen before observing outcomes.

Adapter, generator, validator, and semantics. Execution used adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with declared generator gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json) and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime validator and the post‑hoc scorer. The preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics produced one shared LLM candidate per task that both conditions received; independent_condition_generation was false. This choice intentionally isolates the validator’s accept/block/repair behavior on identical generator outputs rather than exercising generator variance between conditions.

Episode & model‑call accounting. The design planned 800 episodes (2 per task) and allowed up to one repair call per task. Because shared_initial_generation delivered the same LLM candidate to both condition episodes, model_calls_used = 400 (one shared generation per pair) while completed_episode_count = 800. Deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were preregistered: each agent+simulator pair was replayed three times and any non‑identical replays would be flagged and excluded per the preregistered exclusion rules. Exclusion rules and missingness plans were automated; human adjudication was prohibited.

Scoring, repairs, and analysis. The runtime validator applied full intent‑constraint validation; the same validator implementation served as the post‑hoc scorer. The adapter permitted at most one repair call per task; no repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false across episodes). Primary analysis used the preregistered permutation test and corroborating exact McNemar two‑sided check. Secondary/descriptive analyses included paired bootstrap percentile CI for the paired difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and diagnostic cluster analysis of failure traces when present. All analysis code, seeds, and resampling parameters are archived (analysis/*).

Deterministic reproducibility measures. The execution manifest recorded start/completion timestamps, model_calls_used, completed_episode_count, failed_episode_count, and artifact hashes. Deterministic reconciliation confirmed completed_pairs = 400, all deterministic consistency checks passed, and zero exclusions were applied. Key design parameters (task_count=400, maximum_model_calls=800, independent_condition_generation=false) are reported in the preregistration and execution manifest.

The lack of repairs or rollbacks indicates the runtime validator universally accepted the shared candidate outputs produced under shared_initial_generation.

sections.discussion:
Interpretation and construct‑validity diagnosis. The observed null/ceiling outcome is a direct consequence of two preregistered design decisions: (1) shared_initial_generation semantics delivered identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes; and (2) the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Together these choices meant that for every task the shared candidate was accepted by the deterministic validator and the post‑hoc scorer also marked the result correct—producing n_11 = 400 and zero discordant pairs. The experiment therefore measured validator acceptance on identical candidates rather than independent closed‑loop generator+guard dynamics; the primary estimand (paired difference) became uninformative in this run.

Statistical and power implications. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and intra‑pair variability; the observed ceiling invalidates those assumptions. The permutation and exact McNemar tests correctly reflect the observed identical outcomes (p = 1.0). Because the outcome was deterministic and unanimous, uncertainty estimates collapse to degenerate intervals in this run.

Operational implications and guidance for benchmark hardening. The artifact trace and manifest evidence allow concrete recommendations to expose generator×guard dynamics in follow‑on runs: (A) remove shared_initial_generation (set independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives an independently sampled generator output; (B) evaluate heterogeneous pairings (different validator implementations for runtime guard vs. post‑hoc scorer) to avoid scorer/guard conflation; (C) inject adversarial/perturbation seeds that are known to produce invalid or borderline generator outputs on a controlled fraction of tasks; (D) enable and log repair actions in the adapter so that repair_invocation and repair_outcome can produce measurable divergence; (E) include explicit difficulty‑stratified sampling or oversampling of “very_hard” patterns to guarantee non‑trivial baseline error rates for power calculations. These recommendations are implementable starting from archived artifacts (task manifests and response traces) without inventing new datasets.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Model and scope: the run used a single declared generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator; results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity. Environment realism: the benchmark is synthetic and the simulator/validator do not capture all production telemetry noise or adversarial actor behavior. Construct validity: reusing the same deterministic validator as guard and scorer conflates acceptance and scoring. Adversarial robustness remains untested; future designs should include controlled perturbations to probe guard responsiveness.

Reproducibility and artifact placement. All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts referenced in this manuscript: execution/execution_manifest.json (execution summary and model_calls_used), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (paired outcomes), analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg (bootstrap distribution), analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (analysis parameters), and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (full per‑task difficulty labels). These artifacts suffice to reproduce the reported numbers and to seed hardened reruns per the recommendations above.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline and an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the specific generator+validator pairing used, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic runtime validator so both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs; the preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0. This deterministic ceiling outcome stems from preregistered design choices that removed opportunities for the runtime guard to alter outcomes; it does not imply that runtime verification lacks utility in heterogeneous, adversarial, or independent‑generation settings. We release the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts so researchers can reproduce the run and use these artifacts as seeds for hardened experiments that exercise blocking and repair behaviors under independent generation and adversarial perturbations.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl but an aggregated histogram by difficulty level for the full sample was not included in the primary artifacts; readers can derive the complete aggregation from execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the archived bundle. Representative sample difficulty counts (n=6) are included in the Results section to illustrate benchmark diversity.
